body.statement:
Let \(\Gamma\) be a countable finitely generated group with identity \(e\), equipped with a finite symmetric generating set and hence with its bounded-degree vertex-transitive Cayley graph.  Fix a finite set \(A\subset\Gamma\) with \(e\in A\), and declare the finite covariance-support set \(C=AA^{-1}\), with \(a=|A|\) and \(q=|C|\).  Let \(\Lambda\subset\Gamma\) be finite, put
\[
 I=\{v\in\Lambda:vA\subseteq\Lambda\},\qquad
 J_g=\{v\in I:vg\in I\},\qquad
 N=|I|,\qquad \nu=\min_{g\in C}|J_g|,
\]
and suppose \(N>0\) and \(\nu>0\).  Let \((U_v)_{v\in\Gamma}\) be iid with values in a Borel space \(\mathcal U\).  For \(t\in\Gamma\), use the left actions \((t\cdot u)_v=u_{t^{-1}v}\) and \((t\cdot d)_v=d_{t^{-1}v}\).  Conditional on \(\sigma(U)\), let \(D^{(1)}\) and \(D^{(2)}\) be independent, with the coordinates within each wave iid \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_0)\) for a fixed \(p_0\in(0,1)\).

Fix two exposure labels \(c_1,c_0\), a common no-carryover exposure map, and a common no-carryover potential-outcome schedule.  Require both maps to be \(\Gamma\)-equivariant: for all \(t,v\in\Gamma\), environments \(u\), and assignments \(d\),
\[
 E_{tv}(t\cdot d;t\cdot u)=E_v(d;u),
 \qquad
 Y_{tv}(t\cdot d;t\cdot u)=Y_v(d;u).
\]
For the known positive propensities
\[
 \pi_v(c)=\Pr\{E_v(D^{(w)};U)=c\mid\sigma(U)\}>0,
\]
define the exposure-IPW scores explicitly by
\[
 Z_v^{(w)}=Y_v(D^{(w)};U)
 \left\{\frac{\mathbf 1(E_v(D^{(w)};U)=c_1)}{\pi_v(c_1)}
 -\frac{\mathbf 1(E_v(D^{(w)};U)=c_0)}{\pi_v(c_0)}\right\}.
\]
Suppose there is one Borel map
\[
 z:\mathcal U^A\times\{0,1\}^A\longrightarrow[-K_0,K_0],
\]
independent of \(v\) and \(w\), such that, simultaneously for every \(v\in\Gamma\) and \(w\in\{1,2\}\),
\[
 Z_v^{(w)}
 =z\bigl((U_{vx})_{x\in A},(D_{vx}^{(w)})_{x\in A}\bigr)
 \qquad\text{almost surely},
\]
where \(K_0<\infty\).  Define
\[
 m_v=\mathbb E[Z_v^{(w)}\mid\sigma(U)],\quad
 \tau=\mathbb E[m_e],\quad h_v=m_v-\tau,\quad
 \gamma(g)=\mathbb E[h_eh_g],\quad
 \Omega=\sum_{g\in C}\gamma(g),
\]
and, under the common restriction coupling, define
\[
 \overline Z^{(w)}=\frac1N\sum_{v\in I}Z_v^{(w)},\qquad
 \widehat\Omega
 =\sum_{g\in C}\left\{
   \frac1{|J_g|}\sum_{v\in J_g}Z_v^{(1)}Z_{vg}^{(2)}
   -\overline Z^{(1)}\overline Z^{(2)}\right\}.
\]
Then, for every \(g\in C\),
\[
 \mathbb E[Z_v^{(1)}Z_{vg}^{(2)}\mid\sigma(U)]=m_vm_{vg},
\]
and
\[
 \mathbb E[\widehat\Omega]
 =\Omega-q\operatorname{Var}\!\left(N^{-1}\sum_{v\in I}m_v\right),
 \qquad
 0\le \Omega-\mathbb E[\widehat\Omega]
 \le \frac{4q^2K_0^2}{N}. \tag{1}
\]
For every \(\delta\in(0,1)\),
\[
 \Pr\!\left\{
  |\widehat\Omega-\Omega|>
  \frac{4q^2K_0^2}{N}
  +\frac{\sqrt{48|\Lambda|}\,a qK_0^2}{\nu}
    \sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}
 \right\}\le\delta. \tag{2}
\]
If \((\Lambda_j)\) is a right F\o lner sequence, meaning \(|\Lambda_j\mathbin\triangle\Lambda_jg|/|\Lambda_j|\to0\) for every fixed \(g\in\Gamma\), and \(A\), hence \(C\), is fixed, then \(N_j/|\Lambda_j|\to1\), \(\nu_j/|\Lambda_j|\to1\), the bias in (1) is \(O(|\Lambda_j|^{-1})\), and the deviation radius in (2) is \(O(\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/|\Lambda_j|})\).  Thus the fixed-cutoff Palm population-variance diagnostic has root-volume concentration on every such amenable Cayley graph; no growing bandwidth or random graph distance is used.
body.proof_tex:
Let \(\mu_{p_0,A}\) denote the product \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_0)\) law on the finite set \(\{0,1\}^A\), and define the bounded Borel function
\[
 \bar z(u_A)=\sum_{d_A\in\{0,1\}^A}
 z(u_A,d_A)\mu_{p_0,A}(\{d_A\}). \tag{3}
\]
The conditional design law is the fixed product law and does not depend on \(U\).  Consequently, the local-score representation and the defining property of conditional expectation give, for either wave,
\[
 m_v
 =\mathbb E[Z_v^{(w)}\mid\sigma(U)]
 =\bar z((U_{vx})_{x\in A}),
 \qquad |m_v|\le K_0. \tag{4}
\]
In particular, the same \(m_v\) applies to both waves.  Equation (4) also proves, rather than assumes, the required stationarity: for every \(t\in\Gamma\), the array \(((U_{tvx})_{x\in A})_{v\in\Gamma}\) has the same law as \(((U_{vx})_{x\in A})_{v\in\Gamma}\) because the innovation coordinates are iid, and the function \(\bar z\) is independent of \(v\).  Hence \((m_v)_{v\in\Gamma}\) is stationary under left translation and \(\mathbb E[m_v]=\tau\) for every \(v\).

The fixed conditional laws also imply independence of the primitive fields used below.  Indeed, for bounded cylinder functions \(f_0,f_1,f_2\) of \(U,D^{(1)},D^{(2)}\), respectively, conditional wave independence and the fixed product conditional laws yield
\[
 \mathbb E[f_0(U)f_1(D^{(1)})f_2(D^{(2)})]
 =\mathbb E[f_0(U)]
   \int f_1\,d\mu_{p_0}
   \int f_2\,d\mu_{p_0}. \tag{5}
\]
Thus the innovation coordinates, the first-wave assignment coordinates, and the second-wave assignment coordinates form three mutually independent product fields.  The extension from cylinder functions follows from the monotone-class theorem.

If \(vA\cap vgA\ne\varnothing\), then \(vx=vgy\) for some \(x,y\in A\), so \(g=xy^{-1}\in AA^{-1}=C\).  Therefore, when \(g\notin C\), the two innovation blocks in (4) are disjoint.  Independence of the iid innovations and centering of \(h_v=m_v-\tau\) then give
\[
 \mathbb E[h_vh_{vg}]=0\qquad(g\notin C). \tag{6}
\]
This derives the declared covariance support from the common footprint.  It also shows that \(C\) is symmetric and contains \(e\), as follows directly from \(C=AA^{-1}\) and \(e\in A\).

Given \(\sigma(U)\), the first score in a cross-wave product is a function only of \(D^{(1)}\), and the second is a function only of \(D^{(2)}\).  Conditional wave independence, boundedness of \(z\), and (4) therefore imply, for arbitrary \(u,v\in\Gamma\),
\[
 \mathbb E[Z_u^{(1)}Z_v^{(2)}\mid\sigma(U)]
 =\mathbb E[Z_u^{(1)}\mid\sigma(U)]
  \mathbb E[Z_v^{(2)}\mid\sigma(U)]
 =m_um_v. \tag{7}
\]
This proves the first asserted identity, including the case \(u=v\) and all overlapping within-wave footprints.

Stationarity and (7) imply, for every \(g\in C\) and every \(v\in J_g\),
\[
 \mathbb E[Z_v^{(1)}Z_{vg}^{(2)}]
 =\mathbb E[m_vm_{vg}]
 =\tau^2+\mathbb E[h_vh_{vg}]
 =\tau^2+\gamma(g). \tag{8}
\]
Here the last equality translates the pair \((v,vg)\) to \((e,g)\).  Hence averaging (8) over the nonempty set \(J_g\) gives
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[|J_g|^{-1}\sum_{v\in J_g}
 Z_v^{(1)}Z_{vg}^{(2)}\right]=\tau^2+\gamma(g). \tag{9}
\]
Let \(\overline m=N^{-1}\sum_{v\in I}m_v\).  Applying (7) term by term and using \(\mathbb E\overline m=\tau\) gives
\[
 \mathbb E[\overline Z^{(1)}\overline Z^{(2)}]
 =\mathbb E[\overline m^{,2}]
 =\tau^2+\operatorname{Var}(\overline m). \tag{10}
\]
Subtracting \(q\) copies of (10) from the sum of (9) over \(g\in C\) proves
\[
 \mathbb E[\widehat\Omega]
 =\sum_{g\in C}\gamma(g)-q\operatorname{Var}(\overline m)
 =\Omega-q\operatorname{Var}(\overline m). \tag{11}
\]

Since \(|m_v|\le K_0\) and \(|\tau|\le K_0\), one has \(|h_v|\le2K_0\).  For fixed \(u\), relation (6) leaves at most the \(q\) sites \(v=ug\), \(g\in C\), with a possibly nonzero covariance.  Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(\overline m)
 =\frac1{N^2}\sum_{u,v\in I}\mathbb E[h_uh_v]
 \le\frac{Nq\,(2K_0)^2}{N^2}
 =\frac{4qK_0^2}{N}. \tag{12}
\]
Variance nonnegativity, (11), and (12) prove both inequalities in (1).

We next derive finite-sample concentration from the independent primitive coordinates in (5).  Put
\[
 T=\sum_{g\in C}|J_g|^{-1}\sum_{v\in J_g}
 Z_v^{(1)}Z_{vg}^{(2)},
 \qquad
 R=q\overline Z^{(1)}\overline Z^{(2)},
 \qquad
 c=\frac{aqK_0^2}{\nu}, \tag{13}
\]
so that \(\widehat\Omega=T-R\).  A fixed environment coordinate \(U_y\) belongs to at most \(a\) footprints \(vA\), because \(y=vx\) determines \(v=yx^{-1}\) for each \(x\in A\).  At a fixed \(g\), changing \(U_y\) can consequently change at most \(2a\) summands in \(T\), accounting for either endpoint.  Each product lies in \([-K_0^2,K_0^2]\), so
\[
 |\Delta_yT|
 \le\sum_{g\in C}\frac{2a(2K_0^2)}{|J_g|}
 \le\frac{4aqK_0^2}{\nu}=4c. \tag{14}
\]
The same coordinate changes at most \(a\) scores in each wave.  Thus each wave mean changes by at most \(2aK_0/N\), while both old and new wave means lie in \([-K_0,K_0]\).  The product identity \(x'y'-xy=(x'-x)y'+x(y'-y)\) gives
\[
 |\Delta_yR|
 \le q\left(\frac{2aK_0}{N}K_0
             +K_0\frac{2aK_0}{N}\right)
 =\frac{4aqK_0^2}{N}
 \le4c, \tag{15}
\]
where \(\nu\le N\) because every \(J_g\subseteq I\).  Hence one environment coordinate has oscillation at most \(8c\) for \(\widehat\Omega\).

A coordinate \(D_y^{(w)}\) in one assignment wave belongs to at most \(a\) local scores in that wave.  At each \(g\), it therefore changes at most \(a\) products, not \(2a\), because the other factor belongs to the conditionally independent wave.  Repeating (14)--(15) gives
\[
 |\Delta_yT|\le2c,
 \qquad
 |\Delta_yR|\le2c,
 \qquad
 |\Delta_y\widehat\Omega|\le4c. \tag{16}
\]
Every retained score uses only primitive coordinates in \(IA\subseteq\Lambda\); the same is true for both endpoints of every retained product because \(v,vg\in I\).  Thus \(\widehat\Omega\) is a Borel function of at most \(|\Lambda|\) innovation coordinates and at most \(|\Lambda|\) assignment coordinates in each wave.  By (5) these coordinates are independent, and (14)--(16) imply that the sum of their squared oscillation bounds is at most
\[
 |\Lambda|(8c)^2+2|\Lambda|(4c)^2
 =96|\Lambda|c^2. \tag{17}
\]
Apply the frozen McDiarmid bounded-differences lemma, first with all bounds multiplied by \(1+\eta\) and then let \(\eta\downarrow0\) to accommodate its strict oscillation convention.  For every \(t>0\),
\[
 \Pr\{|\widehat\Omega-\mathbb E\widehat\Omega|>t\}
 \le2\exp\!\left\{-\frac{t^2}{48|\Lambda|c^2}\right\}. \tag{18}
\]
Taking
\[
 t=\sqrt{48|\Lambda|}\,c\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)} \tag{19}
\]
makes the right side of (18) equal to \(\delta\).  The deterministic bias bound in (1), (18), (19), and the triangle inequality prove (2).

It remains to verify the F\o lner assertions.  Because \(e\in A\),
\[
 I=\Lambda\cap\bigcap_{x\in A}\Lambda x^{-1}.
\]
For a right F\o lner sequence and fixed finite \(A\), the union bound gives
\[
 \frac{|\Lambda_j\setminus I_j|}{|\Lambda_j|}
 \le\sum_{x\in A}
 \frac{|\Lambda_j\mathbin\triangle\Lambda_jx^{-1}|}{|\Lambda_j|}
 \longrightarrow0. \tag{20}
\]
Consequently \(N_j/|\Lambda_j|\to1\).  For fixed \(g\in C\), translation preserves cardinality and
\[
 |I_j\mathbin\triangle I_jg^{-1}|
 \le2|\Lambda_j\setminus I_j|
   +|\Lambda_j\mathbin\triangle\Lambda_jg^{-1}|. \tag{21}
\]
Since \(J_{j,g}=I_j\cap I_jg^{-1}\), equations (20)--(21) yield \(|J_{j,g}|/|\Lambda_j|\to1\).  The set \(C\) is finite, so taking the minimum gives \(\nu_j/|\Lambda_j|\to1\).  Substitution into (1)--(2), with fixed \(A\), \(a\), and \(q\), proves respectively the \(O(|\Lambda_j|^{-1})\) bias and \(O(\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/|\Lambda_j|})\) deviation radius.

As an exact smallest-instance stress test, take \(A=\{e\}\) and \(\Lambda=\{e\}\).  Then \(C=I=J_e=\{e\}\), \(N=\nu=a=q=1\), and the two terms defining \(\widehat\Omega\) cancel for every realized assignment, so \(\widehat\Omega=0\).  Meanwhile \(\Omega=\operatorname{Var}(m_e)\), and (11) reads exactly \(0=\Omega-\operatorname{Var}(m_e)\).  Thus the expectation identity survives enumeration of every assignment in the smallest finite volume.  The root-volume conclusion deliberately keeps \(A\) fixed and uses \(\nu_j/|\Lambda_j|\to1\); allowing the footprint to grow or the lag-pair interior to collapse would invalidate the final rate substitution and is not claimed.
body.justification: The theorem derives cross-wave identification, the finite-volume centering bias, and root-volume concentration from one common bounded local score rule, rather than assuming stationarity or a limit law.
body.gap: Existing interference results do not provide this fixed-footprint repeated-randomization Palm covariance diagnostic on deterministic F\o lner interiors.
body.consumer: The integer-line theorem is the specialization with \(A=\{-r,\ldots,r\}\); other finitely generated amenable Cayley graphs use the same explicit estimator and constants after replacing interval interiors by footprint interiors.
